noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: explain how the heart rate changes during exercise and under the influence of adrenaline

primer.text: Your heart does not set its own tempo by accident — a patch of cells acts as its conductor, and both exercise and adrenaline speed the music up. This note explains who keeps the beat and why a sprint, or a scare, sends your pulse racing.

lessons.title: The Pacemaker Sets the Tempo
lessons.opening: A cluster of cells in the right atrium, the pacemaker, fires electrical impulses that initiate each contraction of the cardiac muscle and so coordinates the resting heart rate.
keyPoints: Heart rate is counted in beats per minute.
The pacemaker sits in the right atrium.
It sends electrical impulses through the cardiac muscle.
Those impulses initiate and coordinate each contraction.
Exercise and adrenaline both lift the tempo above resting.

low.restatement: The pacemaker in the right atrium sparks each beat and keeps the rhythm steady.
low.analogy: A drummer setting the beat for the whole band.
low.examPointer: Location matters: right atrium, not left, and the signals are electrical.

medium.restatement: Because the impulses spread from one authority, atria and ventricles contract in an ordered sequence rather than randomly.
medium.analogy: One conductor's baton keeps forty players in time; without it, chaos.
medium.examPointer: Use the word 'coordinate' when explaining the pacemaker's role — it is the mark scheme's verb.

check.stem: Where is the heart's natural pacemaker located?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
The ventricle contracts; it does not set the tempo.
The aorta is an exit vessel, not a rhythm setter.
The septum separates sides; the pacemaker sits in the right atrium.

check.stem: What do pacemaker cells send out to start a contraction?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Adrenaline is hormonal; the pacemaker works electrically.
Oxygen arrives by blood, not from the pacemaker.
The signal is electrical, later becoming mechanical.

check.stem: In what unit is heart rate expressed?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Far too slow a unit for a living pulse.
That is a flow volume, not a beat count.
That unit measures blood pressure.

check.stem: What role does the pacemaker play in keeping the beat?

options.text: It regulates the heart rate and coordinates the contraction of the cardiac muscle
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: It filters the blood passing through
options.explanation: No filtering happens in the atrium.

options.text: It stores oxygen for the muscle
options.explanation: Storage is not a heart role.
Adrenaline comes from glands, not the pacemaker.

check.stem: Which two factors are named as raisers of the heart rate?

options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Sleep lowers the rate; hydration has no such effect.
Neither is the named pair here.
Calm states leave the resting rate untouched.

check.stem: State where the pacemaker sits and what it does.
check.modelAnswer: It sits in the right atrium and coordinates the contraction of the heart muscle, regulating the heart rate.
It is the number of times the heart beats in a minute.

check.stem: Explain why impulses from one region keep the heart beating in an orderly sequence.
check.modelAnswer: Because every contraction is initiated from the same pacemaker, the electrical spread follows a fixed route, so atria and ventricles contract in the proper order.

check.stem: An athlete's resting rate sits at 50 beats per minute. Use the pacemaker idea to explain what a coach measures.
check.modelAnswer: The coach is counting the beats per minute set by the athlete's pacemaker; a low resting value reflects an efficient pump rather than a faulty conductor.

lessons.title: Exercise, Adrenaline and the Oxygen Debt
lessons.opening: Working muscles respire faster, demanding more oxygen and glucose and quicker carbon dioxide removal, so the heart answers by beating faster and pumping a larger volume per beat — and adrenaline can trigger the same response without any exercise.
keyPoints: Exercising muscles respire faster and need more oxygen and glucose.
The heart rate rises to deliver supplies and clear carbon dioxide.
The blood volume pumped per beat also increases.
After exercise the rate stays high to repay the oxygen debt.
Adrenaline raises the rate as part of fight or flight.

low.restatement: Hard work raises the pulse; afterwards it lingers high while lactic acid is cleared.
low.analogy: A restaurant kitchen: more orders (exercise) means faster deliveries, and the washing-up continues after closing.
low.examPointer: Tie the lingering pulse to lactic acid breakdown — that is the oxygen debt.

medium.restatement: Both delivery rate and per-beat volume rise, so oxygen and glucose reach the muscles per minute in the quantity their faster respiration demands.
medium.analogy: Widening a motorway and letting more cars onto it at once, so supplies arrive sooner.
medium.examPointer: For 'explain the rise' questions, name both changes: heart rate AND volume per beat.

check.stem: Why do muscle cells need a faster blood supply during exercise?

options.text: They respire faster, demanding more oxygen and glucose and quicker waste removal
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: They stop respiring to save energy
options.explanation: Respiration accelerates rather than stops.

options.text: They need less oxygen when active
options.explanation: Activity raises the demand, not lowers it.

options.text: Blood supplies them with adrenaline only
options.explanation: Adrenaline is a signal, not the muscle's fuel.

check.stem: Which two responses does the heart make during exercise?

options.text: It beats faster and pumps a larger volume per beat
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Slowing would starve the muscles.
No pausing occurs during exercise.

options.text: It pumps less per beat to save energy
options.explanation: Per-beat volume increases, not decreases.

check.stem: Why does heart rate stay high after exercise ends?

options.text: To supply the oxygen that breaks down the lactic acid built during the oxygen-free route
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Cooling is not the named reason.
Adrenaline fades; the debt is the driver.
The muscles are recovering, not resting, during this period.

check.stem: What may muscle cells do when oxygen supply cannot meet demand in intense exercise?

options.text: Add anaerobic respiration alongside the still-running aerobic route
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Energy demand continues; cells never stop.
Animal cells cannot photosynthesise.

options.text: Store glucose instead of using it
options.explanation: Storage would starve the contraction.

check.stem: How does adrenaline raise the heart rate?

options.text: As the hormone behind fight or flight, readying the body for sudden action
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Walls do not thicken on demand.

options.text: By adding glucose to the blood directly
options.explanation: Adrenaline signals; it is not a fuel.

options.text: By slowing digestion to a stop
options.explanation: Digestion changes, but the rate rises through the pacemaker.

check.stem: State what the heart supplies to respiring muscles and removes from them.
check.modelAnswer: It supplies oxygen and glucose for respiration and removes carbon dioxide.

check.stem: Name the hormone that raises heart rate without exercise.
check.modelAnswer: Adrenaline, the fight-or-flight hormone, lifts the heart rate ahead of action.

check.stem: Explain why both heart rate and per-beat volume must rise together in exercise.
check.modelAnswer: Because the muscles' faster respiration needs more oxygen and glucose delivered per minute, and one mechanism alone could not move enough blood to meet that demand.

check.stem: A sprinter's pulse is still high two minutes after finishing. Explain the physiology.
check.modelAnswer: The sprint added anaerobic respiration in the leg muscles, building lactic acid; the raised heart rate supplies the oxygen needed to break that lactic acid down, repaying the oxygen debt.

glossary.definition: The cell cluster in the right atrium that initiates each heartbeat electrically.
The number of heartbeats counted in one minute.
The fight-or-flight hormone that raises heart rate ahead of action.
The post-exercise oxygen needed to break down accumulated lactic acid.
